topic: Physics grew out of ancient astronomy, optics and mechanics; Greek philosophers sought natural causes, and Aristotle's system dominated for nearly 2,000 years.
Scholars of the medieval Islamic world preserved and advanced this work, notably in optics.
The Scientific Revolution (Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler, Newton) replaced it with experiment and mathematical laws; Newton's mechanics and gravity explained heaven and earth alike.
19th-century physics unified electricity, magnetism and light, and founded thermodynamics; relativity and quantum mechanics in the 20th century then rebuilt the foundations.

Ancient history: Babylonians and Egyptians made careful astronomical observations; Greek thinkers from Thales on looked for natural rather than divine explanations.
Democritus proposed atoms; Aristotle's physics of natural motion and four elements lasted until the 17th century.
In the Hellenistic period Archimedes founded statics and hydrostatics, and Aristarchus proposed a sun-centred cosmos.
Medieval science: Scholars in the Islamic world translated and extended Greek work; Ibn al-Haytham's 'Book of Optics' explained vision by light entering the eye and used experiment.
Al-Biruni, Avicenna and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi advanced astronomy and mechanics; Shen Kuo described the magnetic compass in China.
In Europe, scholastics such as Buridan developed 'impetus' theory, a step toward the idea of inertia.
Scientific Revolution: Copernicus (1543) put the Sun at the centre; Tycho Brahe's observations let Kepler find that planets move in ellipses.
Galileo used the telescope and experiments on falling bodies and was condemned by the Church (1633).
Descartes, Gilbert, Torricelli and others pursued mechanical and experimental explanations.
Newton's Principia (1687) set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation, uniting terrestrial and celestial mechanics.
18th-century developments: Euler, Lagrange and others rewrote Newton's mechanics in powerful mathematical form; Bernoulli founded fluid dynamics.
Franklin, Cavendish and Volta studied electricity; Volta built the first battery (1800).
Black and Lavoisier studied heat and chemistry, laying groundwork for thermodynamics.
19th century: Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction; Maxwell's equations (1860s) unified electricity, magnetism and light as electromagnetic waves.
Joule, Mayer and Helmholtz established the conservation of energy; thermodynamics and statistical mechanics explained heat as molecular motion.
Fresnel's wave theory of light won out, Foucault measured the speed of light, and Röntgen discovered X-rays (1895).
20th century: birth of modern physics: Planck's quantum (1900) and Einstein's light quanta (1905) began quantum theory; Einstein's relativity (1905, 1915) reshaped space, time and gravity.
Thomson discovered the electron; Rutherford found the nucleus; Bohr, Schrödinger, Heisenberg, Pauli and Dirac built quantum mechanics in the 1920s.
Meitner and others discovered nuclear fission (1938); quantum electrodynamics (Feynman and others) and the electroweak theory (Weinberg and others) followed.
Contemporary physics: The Standard Model describes the known particles and three of the four forces; the Higgs boson was confirmed in 2012.
Physical cosmology studies the Big Bang, dark matter and dark energy.
Unifying gravity with quantum theory remains the great open problem.
